title: Two-Parameter Flows for Learning Population Dynamics of Physical Systems
claim: Two coupled flows on one shared base point: a learnable sampling-time transport implicitly defines a physics-time dynamic, so learning one lets us predict the other.
layout: 1 panel, base point at bottom, two curves up, arrows at endpoints
description: A single geometric sketch on a white background. A black dot labeled bold a sits at the bottom, with two black curves rising from it to two black dots at upper left and upper right. The left dot is labeled x_{t,s} = Φ(a,t,s), and the right dot is x_{t',s}. A third black arc connects the two upper dots across the top. At each upper dot, a blue arrow points up and is labeled v(x, t, s), the sampling-time velocity. A crimson arrow points sideways along the top arc and is labeled u(x, t, s), the physics-time velocity. Blue and crimson color-code the vertical and horizontal flows. The eye goes first to the colored arrows and equations at the top, then down to the base point a.
caption: Learn vertically, predict horizontally: The vertical flow in sampling time s along v : ∂sΦ = v ◦Φ is learned through existing, scalable methods from generative modeling. After training, we have implicitly defined a horizontal flow u ◦Φ = ∂tΦ which we can make explicit in a second regression step and use for rapid inference in physics time t.
abstract: This work addresses the problem of learning the dynamics of high-dimensional probability densities over time using unlabeled samples, without assuming access to trajectory information. We introduce two-parameter flows that learn only sampling-time transports from a base distribution to each marginal and then extract a physics-time velocity by regressing on coupled synthetic trajectories. We prove that the resulting physics-time dynamics are unique and inherit regularity from the sampling-time transports. Because we can build on standard, well-developed conditional flow matching techniques for learning the base-to-marginal transports, our approach scales to high dimensions and avoids per-step optimal-transport couplings, while allowing admissible non-gradient dynamics that can naturally explain rotational or circulating physics phenomena.
